items.title: Old FireWire Audio Interface Gets USB C Upgrade
items.summary: [bonsembiante] had a PreSonus Firestudio Project on hand. It’s a very capable audio interface with 8 inputs and 8 outputs, along with MIDI to boot. However, it’s got one problem—it runs on FireWire. To bring it into modernity, the device would need an upgrade to USB operation . This would be no mean feat. [bonsembiante] decided to remove the original FireWire controller hardware entirely, replacing it with an XMOS-based USB audio setup while reusing the existing audio circuitry in the interface. The trick was figuring out where all the digital audio signals were on the original board, and wiring them into the XMOS board with an interleaved ground-signal pattern with equal length conductors to avoid issues with interference and jitter. With the modern XMOS board hacked into the older hardware, all that was then required were the right drivers to get modern machines accessing all 8 ins and outs via a USB C connection. Files are on Github for the curious. The hope is to turn this into a broader project that can be used on a range of older FireWire-based audio interfaces. To that end, [bonsembiante] has an explainer page on the goals and purpose of the fuegocable effort. The next interfaces targeted by the project are the Presonus FP10 and Focusrite Saffire. We’ve featured [bonsembiante’s] work before, too, like this ADSL modem repurposed as a guitar effects pedal . Video after the break. As someone still using an RME Fireface 400 as their daily driver with a pci-e FireWire card, this direction is very intriguing. items.title: This Week In Security: Java4Shell, Optimizely Malware, Shrinking Disclosure Deadlines, Unpatchable Freezers
items.summary: Last month, the details of PHP2Shell leaked before the embargo lifted, and PHP had to scramble its release out early . This week, the same research firm, Calif, had it happen again, this time with Java. Java4Shell ( CVE-2026-114938 ) is a heap overflow in OpenJDK’s hardware-accelerated Base64 decoder, and on November 17, Calif said it was going public early because the vulnerability had leaked. Oracle and OpenJDK pushed fixes that afternoon, and Calif followed with its write-up . Java normally runs virtual bytecode inside the Java virtual machine, but when a function gets called often enough, the HotSpot JIT compiler turns it into native code. For some common operations it goes a step further, and swaps in hand-tuned machine code which uses special CPU instructions. On x86-64 CPUs with AVX-512 instructions, Base64 decoding is one of those, chewing through 64 bytes at a time with a mask that decides which output bytes actually get written. When the last chunk of input is a short, malformed tail with “=” padding, the calculated output length underflows below zero, the mask ends up with every bit set, and the decoder writes 64 bytes where it should have written at most two. Java then correctly throws an exception for the bad input, but by then, 62 bytes past the end of the output buffer have already been overwritten. The overwritten bytes are fixed; the attacker controls when and where the write happens, but not what is written. Calif turned that into a working exploit anyhow. The overflow overwrites the length field of a nearby array, which allows for overwriting more of the heap with chosen values, and then into a way to read heap memory back in a response, which may hold keys, tokens, and other secrets. items.summary: A2UI 1.0 is an open protocol for generative UI that enables AI agents to render interactive, native screens across web, mobile, and desktop applications. Developers can leverage open-source renderer SDKs—including React, Angular, Lit, Flutter, SwiftUI, and Jetpack Compose—alongside agent SDKs for Python, TypeScript, and Dart. The release introduces bidirectional function calls, swappable inference formats, and secure data binding to help teams seamlessly integrate generative UI into their product stacks.

items.title: On-Device Speech Recognition and Text-to-Speech in Google AI Edge Gallery
items.summary: Google AI Edge Gallery now supports on-device, offline Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) and Text-to-Speech (TTS) capabilities for building developer-friendly voice applications. Developers can leverage ML Kit for optimized Android performance, or use MediaPipe Tasks and LiteRT for cross-platform open-weight model integration. This local pipeline seamlessly pairs lightweight speech models with on-device small language models like Gemini Nano and Gemma 4 to enable real-time streaming transcription and low-latency synthesis.

items.title: Announcing Long-Context Training on TPUs with MaxText Context Parallelism
items.summary: Google Cloud's MaxText framework now supports long-context training up to 14 million tokens on Cloud TPUs by implementing four context-parallel strategies: All-gather, A2A, P2P, and USP. Powered by the Tokamax Splash Attention kernel, these strategies effectively manage attention compute and memory bottlenecks without materializing full key-value sequences in high-bandwidth memory. Developers can adopt these capabilities in MaxText v0.2.4 to achieve high Model FLOPs Utilization (MFU) across large-scale model training workflows.

items.title: From prompt to app: Build with Google Maps in AI Studio
items.summary: Developers can now build applications powered by Google Maps Platform directly within Google AI Studio by prompting Gemini with real-world geospatial concepts. The integration eliminates traditional configuration hurdles by providing one-click demo keys that generate instantly without requiring Cloud Console redirects or credit cards. This setup grants developers immediate access to core APIs—including Maps, Places, and Routes—supported by daily sandbox quotas for seamless prototyping.

items.title: What is Pathways? Single-controller training for large models
items.summary: Pathways is a single-controller distributed training system designed to coordinate large-scale model training across multiple accelerator groups by representing computations as a global dataflow graph. Unlike traditional SPMD models like DDP and FSDP that rely on synchronous collectives, Pathways uses asynchronous dispatch and a central scheduler to maximize hardware utilization and prevent deadlocks in complex workloads. By decoupling model definition from physical hardware via virtual devices, developers can efficiently scale complex training architectures and seamlessly handle dynamic workloads like reinforcement learning post-training.
